Good. Two things are now clear:

  1. Your repo settings are fine.

  2. git fetch origin succeeded, so the network and GitHub access are working.

That means you are in a good state to pull the team leader’s changes. GitHub’s docs say HTTPS Git operations use a personal access token or credential helper rather than a password, and cached credentials can cause failures if they are stale. GitHub Docs+2GitHub Docs+2

Do this now

First, confirm what branch origin/main is on:

PowerShell
git log --oneline --decorate --graph --all -10

Then, because your local main is already ahead by your image-model commit, the cleanest next step is:

PowerShell
git checkout -b image-model-final
git push -u origin image-model-final

If pushing still prompts for credentials, GitHub recommends using a personal access token over HTTPS, or re-authenticating through Git Credential Manager. When Git asks for a password, enter the token instead of your account password. GitHub Docs+2GitHub Docs+2

Then pull your team leader’s changes

Once the branch is safe on GitHub, go back to main and pull:

PowerShell
git checkout main
git pull origin main

If Git says your local branch and remote branch diverged, use:

PowerShell
git pull --rebase origin main

Important

Your current local commit is safe. Do not reset anything yet.

If you want the shortest path, do this sequence exactly:

PowerShell
git checkout -b image-model-final
git push -u origin image-model-final
git checkout main
git pull origin main

If the push fails again, the issue is authentication, not the code. GitHub’s docs recommend using a PAT over HTTPS or refreshing the credential cache in Git Credential Manager. GitHub Docs+2GitHub Docs+2
